sentences.text: The holotype skull measured 154 mm in length and weighed an estimated seven pounds, while the entire animal was small, weighing around 3 kg.
It possessed only jugal horns and a small frill, lacking the orbital horns and neck shield seen in later ceratopsians.
The small frill on the back of the skull had clear marks for the insertion of chewing muscles.
The small frill on the back of Liaoceratops's skull had clear marks for the insertion of chewing muscles.
Liaoceratops had a small horn sheath on each side below its eyes.
A referred juvenile skull lacked its skull roof, which researchers explain as the result of a predator breaking the braincase to eat the contents.
The genus Liaoceratops was described by Xu and colleagues in 2002 after being discovered in China by a team of American and Chinese scientists.
The species Liaoceratops yanzigouensis was named and described in 2002 by Xu Xing, Peter Makovicky, Wang Xiaolin, Mark Norell, and You Hailu.
The holotype specimen IVPP V12738 was found in the Barremian-aged Yixian Formation, and in 2007, a skull of an even younger individual, specimen CAGS-IG-VD-002, was referred to the species.
There are currently two recorded fossil occurrences of Liaoceratops in the scientific database.
Liaoceratops possessed an excellent sense of smell due to having large olfactory bulbs relative to its size.
Short cochlear ducts suggest Liaoceratops individuals communicated through high-frequency vocalizations.
Anatomical features suggest Liaoceratops had an almost horizontal head posture and was bipedal.
Liaoceratops belongs to the family Archaeoceratopsidae.
Liaoceratops belongs to the parent group Neoceratopsia.
Liaoceratops is classified within the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
Liaoceratops lived approximately 126 million years ago during the Early Cretaceous.
It lived at the beginning of the Cretaceous period, approximately 126 million years ago, in the Barremian stage in what is now Asia.
Liaoceratops lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, from 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago.
Liaoceratops inhabited forest and wetland environments of the Jehol Biota during the Early Cretaceous.
While initially thought to be offensive or defensive organs, many paleontologists now consider Liaoceratops's horns and frill to be display devices used for species recognition and attracting mates.
